A 2025 meta-analysis covering more than 2.5 million people found that people who trust others more consistently report greater well-being — and the relationship appears to feed itself. Longitudinal studies showed that trust predicts greater future well-being, while greater well-being predicts more future trust, creating what researchers describe as a mutually reinforcing cycle.

Edited by Lachlan Brown

Trust is often described as a virtue, a personality trait or a risky decision. A large 2025 meta-analysis suggests it is also connected to how people experience their lives. Across hundreds of studies, people who reported greater trust in other people and institutions consistently tended to report better subjective well-being.

Keep Watching
A 2025 meta-analysis covering more than 2.5 million people found that people who trust others more consistently report greater well-being — and the relationship appears to feed itself. Longitudinal studies showed that trust predicts greater future well-being, while greater well-being predicts more future trust, creating what researchers describe as a mutually reinforcing cycle.A 2025 meta-analysis covering more than 2.5 million people found that people who trust others more consistently report greater well-being — and the relationship appears to feed itself. Longitudinal studies showed that trust predicts greater future well-being, while greater well-being predicts more future trust, creating what researchers describe as a mutually reinforcing cycle.
Watch More

The most interesting result was not the basic association. Longitudinal studies showed movement in both directions. Higher trust predicted slightly better well-being later, even after earlier well-being was taken into account. Higher well-being likewise predicted slightly more trust later. The researchers described this as a mutually reinforcing cycle.

That language is justified, but it needs boundaries. The effects over time were small, and the studies were observational. The evidence supports a reciprocal pattern. It does not prove that trust alone causes happiness, or that telling someone to trust more will improve a difficult life.

A synthesis of 2,518,769 people

The Psychological Bulletin meta-analysis was preregistered and followed PRISMA reporting guidelines. It included 241 reports containing 488 studies, which together produced 991 usable effect sizes and represented 2,518,769 participants. The authors made their plan, coding materials and analysis resources available through an Open Science Framework project.

Many effect sizes came from large data sources such as the World Values Survey, which generated samples across countries and cohorts. The researchers therefore used a four-level random-effects model. That approach accounted for ordinary sampling error, multiple estimates from one study, different studies drawing from a shared data source, and variation between data sources.

The studies ranged across Europe, Asia, North America, Oceania, Africa and South America. Participants’ mean ages ran from about six to nearly 84, although children, younger adolescents and the oldest adults were relatively underrepresented. Most samples came from the general population, while others included people affected by illness, displacement, disasters and other vulnerabilities.

The overall relationship was consistent, not enormous

The pooled cross-sectional correlation between trust and subjective well-being was (r=.21), with a 95 percent confidence interval from .19 to .23. Removing 16 statistical outliers barely changed it. A correlation of .21 is meaningful across a population, but it is modest. Squared, it represents roughly 4 percent shared variance, so most differences in well-being were associated with other factors.

The finding also was not one survey asking one question. The review covered generalized trust in people broadly, interpersonal trust in known people and institutional trust. Subjective well-being included life satisfaction, positive emotion, negative emotion and combined measures.

The full published analysis found the association across every sample and study characteristic examined. Its size nevertheless varied substantially between studies. The relationship was robust in direction, not identical in every setting.

The longitudinal evidence ran both ways

A one-time survey cannot tell whether trust comes before well-being, well-being comes before trust, or both reflect a third factor. The researchers therefore conducted separate longitudinal meta-analyses using cross-lagged estimates.

Fifty-five effect sizes tested whether trust predicted subsequent well-being. The mean regression coefficient was (B=.07), with a 95 percent confidence interval from .05 to .09. Forty-nine effect sizes tested the reverse direction. Well-being predicted subsequent trust at (B=.06), with a 95 percent confidence interval from .04 to .08.

These models controlled for prior levels of the later outcome and for the initial cross-sectional association between the two variables. In other words, the first result asked whether trust predicted later well-being beyond where well-being started, while the second asked whether well-being predicted later trust beyond where trust started. The time between assessments did not significantly change either pooled relationship.

The coefficients were small, yet their similar size and opposite directions make the cyclical interpretation plausible. Earlier cross-national work using representative samples from 18 societies also examined the relationship with cross-lagged panel analysis, reflecting the broader effort to move beyond a single-time association.

Not every kind of trust carried the same weight

Interpersonal trust had the strongest cross-sectional association with subjective well-being at (r=.25). Generalized trust followed at (r=.20), while institutional trust had the weakest association at (r=.17). The differences were statistically meaningful but not vast.

Trust was also more strongly related to life satisfaction, (r=.23), than to positive affect, (r=.20), or negative affect, (r=.19). That distinction makes sense without proving a mechanism. Trust may contribute to a durable sense that life is stable, supported and predictable, while daily emotions are more responsive to immediate events.

Age mattered. The relationship was stronger among children and adolescents than among early and middle-aged adults, and it was also relatively strong among older adults. National context mattered too: individual trust was more closely associated with well-being in countries where generalized trust was more common.

That last result is important. A trusting person may benefit more when the surrounding environment is actually cooperative. Trust is not just an internal attitude. It is partly a response to whether other people and institutions behave reliably.

Why “mutually reinforcing” is not the same as causal proof

The longitudinal pattern improves on a simple correlation, but it remains observational. Unmeasured variables could influence both sides of the cycle. Stable relationships, personality, physical health, financial security, social support and safe institutions might make a person both more trusting and more satisfied.

Most of the underlying studies were not designed primarily to eliminate those alternatives. Some controlled for demographics, social networks, social capital, support or personality. In a few, an association weakened or disappeared after additional controls were introduced. The review found only three longitudinal studies examining mechanisms between trust and later well-being, or the reverse, and all used just two waves of data. At least three waves are generally needed for a stronger test of mediation.

The authors also detected a possible publication-bias signal in the cross-sectional literature. Positive findings may be more likely to be published. They found no comparable signal in the longitudinal analyses, but absence of that warning is not the same as experimental proof.

Earlier work using the Gallup World Poll and Canadian survey data likewise found substantial links between trust and well-being. The new meta-analysis makes the combined evidence much harder to dismiss, while still leaving the causal machinery unresolved.

Trust has to be earned by people and institutions

The findings are not an instruction to trust indiscriminately. Trust always has a target: a friend, partner, stranger, employer, court, government or process. Its benefits depend partly on whether that target is genuinely trustworthy. Confidence placed in a deceptive person or an unaccountable institution can create vulnerability rather than well-being.

This distinction gives the research particular relevance to law and public institutions. Legitimacy is not created by demanding public confidence. It grows from transparent procedures, consistent rules, fair treatment, meaningful review and accountability when power is misused. The paper itself points to transparency and fairness in policy, an independent press and a transparent judiciary as conditions that can support trustworthiness.

The same reciprocal logic can apply at a smaller scale. Dependable relationships make trust more reasonable, while trust can make cooperation and closeness easier. The Law Dictionary has previously examined how the long-running Harvard Study of Adult Development connected close relationships with later health and happiness.

The careful conclusion is not that trust is a switch for happiness. It is that trust and well-being show a durable positive relationship, and small prospective effects run in both directions. A healthier cycle seems possible when people feel better able to rely on others, and when the people and institutions around them give that reliance a sound basis.

This article provides general information about behavioral research and is not legal or psychological advice.

Data preferences

Manage your data

You can choose how your personal data is used. Vendors want your permission to do the following:

Purposes

Store and/or access information on a device

Cookies, device or similar online identifiers (e.g. login-based identifiers, randomly assigned identifiers, network based identifiers) together with other information (e.g. browser type and information, language, screen size, supported technologies etc.) can be stored or read on your device to recognise it each time it connects to an app or to a website, for one or several of the purposes presented here.

View details

Use limited data to select advertising

Advertising presented to you on this service can be based on limited data, such as the website or app you are using, your non-precise location, your device type or which content you are (or have been) interacting with (for example, to limit the number of times an ad is presented to you).

View details

Create profiles for personalised advertising

Information about your activity on this service (such as forms you submit, content you look at) can be stored and combined with other information about you (for example, information from your previous activity on this service and other websites or apps) or similar users. This is then used to build or improve a profile about you (that might include possible interests and personal aspects). Your profile can be used (also later) to present advertising that appears more relevant based on your possible interests by this and other entities.

View details

Use profiles to select personalised advertising

Advertising presented to you on this service can be based on your advertising profiles, which can reflect your activity on this service or other websites or apps (like the forms you submit, content you look at), possible interests and personal aspects.

View details

Create profiles to personalise content

Information about your activity on this service (for instance, forms you submit, non-advertising content you look at) can be stored and combined with other information about you (such as your previous activity on this service or other websites or apps) or similar users. This is then used to build or improve a profile about you (which might for example include possible interests and personal aspects). Your profile can be used (also later) to present content that appears more relevant based on your possible interests, such as by adapting the order in which content is shown to you, so that it is even easier for you to find content that matches your interests.

View details

Use profiles to select personalised content

Content presented to you on this service can be based on your content personalisation profiles, which can reflect your activity on this or other services (for instance, the forms you submit, content you look at), possible interests and personal aspects. This can for example be used to adapt the order in which content is shown to you, so that it is even easier for you to find (non-advertising) content that matches your interests.

View details

Measure advertising performance

Information regarding which advertising is presented to you and how you interact with it can be used to determine how well an advert has worked for you or other users and whether the goals of the advertising were reached. For instance, whether you saw an ad, whether you clicked on it, whether it led you to buy a product or visit a website, etc. This is very helpful to understand the relevance of advertising campaigns.

View details

Measure content performance

Information regarding which content is presented to you and how you interact with it can be used to determine whether the (non-advertising) content e.g. reached its intended audience and matched your interests. For instance, whether you read an article, watch a video, listen to a podcast or look at a product description, how long you spent on this service and the web pages you visit etc. This is very helpful to understand the relevance of (non-advertising) content that is shown to you.

View details

Understand audiences through statistics or combinations of data from different sources

Reports can be generated based on the combination of data sets (like user profiles, statistics, market research, analytics data) regarding your interactions and those of other users with advertising or (non-advertising) content to identify common characteristics (for instance, to determine which target audiences are more receptive to an ad campaign or to certain contents).

View details

Develop and improve services

Information about your activity on this service, such as your interaction with ads or content, can be very helpful to improve products and services and to build new products and services based on user interactions, the type of audience, etc. This specific purpose does not include the development or improvement of user profiles and identifiers.

View details

Use limited data to select content

Content presented to you on this service can be based on limited data, such as the website or app you are using, your non-precise location, your device type, or which content you are (or have been) interacting with (for example, to limit the number of times a video or an article is presented to you).

View details

Special purposes

Ensure security, prevent and detect fraud, and fix errors

Your data can be used to monitor for and prevent unusual and possibly fraudulent activity (for example, regarding advertising, ad clicks by bots), and ensure systems and processes work properly and securely. It can also be used to correct any problems you, the publisher or the advertiser may encounter in the delivery of content and ads and in your interaction with them.

View details

Deliver and present advertising and content

Certain information (like an IP address or device capabilities) is used to ensure the technical compatibility of the content or advertising, and to facilitate the transmission of the content or ad to your device.

View details

Save and communicate privacy choices

The choices you make regarding the purposes and entities listed in this notice are saved and made available to those entities in the form of digital signals (such as a string of characters). This is necessary in order to enable both this service and those entities to respect such choices.

View details

Features

These means of processing can be used solely in pursuit of one or several purposes for which you are given a choice in this notice.

Match and combine data from other data sources

Information about your activity on this service may be matched and combined with other information relating to you and originating from various sources (for instance your activity on a separate online service, your use of a loyalty card in-store, or your answers to a survey), in support of the purposes explained in this notice.

View details

Link different devices

In support of the purposes explained in this notice, your device might be considered as likely linked to other devices that belong to you or your household (for instance because you are logged in to the same service on both your phone and your computer, or because you may use the same Internet connection on both devices).

View details

Identify devices based on information transmitted automatically

Your device might be distinguished from other devices based on information it automatically sends when accessing the Internet (for instance, the IP address of your Internet connection or the type of browser you are using) in support of the purposes exposed in this notice.

View details

Special features

Use precise geolocation data

With your acceptance, your precise location (within a radius of less than 500 metres) may be used in support of the purposes explained in this notice.

View details

Identify devices based on information actively requested

With your acceptance, certain characteristics specific to your device might be requested and used to distinguish it from other devices (such as the installed fonts or plugins, the resolution of your screen) in support of the purposes explained in this notice.

How this consent management platform (CMP) works:

CMP privacy choices

Storage, duration, and usage details

The choices you make with this CMP regarding the purposes and entities will affect how personalized advertising is presented to you. We need to store these choices to respect them on future visits, and they are stored differently based on the type of site or app you're using:
  • For sites, your choices are saved in a cookie named “FCCDCF” for a maximum duration of 390 days.
  • For apps, your choices are saved in device storage prefixed by “IABTCF_”. Your choices will be invalidated after 390 days and overwritten once you make new privacy choices on this app.
  • For accelerated mobile page (AMP) sites, your choices are saved in local storage prefixed by “amp-store”. Your choices will be invalidated after 390 days and overwritten once you make new privacy choices on this site.

Vendor preferences

Vendors can use your data to provide services. Declining a vendor can stop them from using the data you shared.
